tools.name: configuration_view

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: helm_uninstall

name.description: Name of the Helm release to uninstall

namespace.description: Namespace to uninstall the Helm release from (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

tools.name: namespaces_list

tools.name: nodes_log

Done. Here’s what I set up in canary-deployment-ns:

What I deployed
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container name: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80 (matching the stable deployment)
  - Security configuration: same as stable (no explicit securityContext changes)

Traffic routing (about 50/50)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select app=recommendation-engine (removed the version=v2.0 filter), so it targets both the stable (v2.0) and canary (v2.1) pods.
- Service port config preserved: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (unchanged).
- With 2 replicas in each deployment, this yields approximately 50% traffic to the canary.

Current state (quick check)
- Pods running: 2x engine-v2-0 and 2x engine-v2-1 (all Ready)
- Service endpoints now include all four pods (two from v2.0 and two from v2.1) on port 8080.

Notes and rollback
- If you need to roll back traffic immediately to stable only: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.
- To adjust canary weight without changing the Service, change replica counts (e.g., scale canary or stable replicas). Services distribute roughly evenly across ready endpoints.

namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done. Here’s what I set up in canary-deployment-ns:

What I deployed
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container name: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80 (matching the stable deployment)
  - Security configuration: same as stable (no explicit securityContext changes)

Traffic routing (about 50/50)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select app=recommendation-engine (removed the version=v2.0 filter), so it targets both the stable (v2.0) and canary (v2.1) pods.
- Service port config preserved: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (unchanged).
- With 2 replicas in each deployment, this yields approximately 50% traffic to the canary.

Current state (quick check)
- Pods running: 2x engine-v2-0 and 2x engine-v2-1 (all Ready)
- Service endpoints now include all four pods (two from v2.0 and two from v2.1) on port 8080.

Notes and rollback
- If you need to roll back traffic immediately to stable only: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.
- To adjust canary weight without changing the Service, change replica counts (e.g., scale canary or stable replicas). Services distribute roughly evenly across ready endpoints.

outputSteps.content:
Done. Here’s what I set up in canary-deployment-ns:

What I deployed
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container name: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80 (matching the stable deployment)
  - Security configuration: same as stable (no explicit securityContext changes)

Traffic routing (about 50/50)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select app=recommendation-engine (removed the version=v2.0 filter), so it targets both the stable (v2.0) and canary (v2.1) pods.
- Service port config preserved: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (unchanged).
- With 2 replicas in each deployment, this yields approximately 50% traffic to the canary.

Current state (quick check)
- Pods running: 2x engine-v2-0 and 2x engine-v2-1 (all Ready)
- Service endpoints now include all four pods (two from v2.0 and two from v2.1) on port 8080.

Notes and rollback
- If you need to roll back traffic immediately to stable only: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.
- To adjust canary weight without changing the Service, change replica counts (e.g., scale canary or stable replicas). Services distribute roughly evenly across ready endpoints.

outputSteps.content:
I found the issue: the container was started with command/args set to run “/bin/sh -c nonexistent_command”, which caused a CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed:
- Recreated the Deployment without the custom command/args so the image uses its default entrypoint.
- Kept the same image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) and set containerPort to 8080 (the default port for the unprivileged image).

Current status:
- Deployment app (namespace crashloop-test) is healthy: 1/1 replicas Available.
- Pod app-6866cfb945-nrbrt is Running with 0 restarts.

Note: If you have a Service pointing to this Deployment, ensure its targetPort is 8080 (the unprivileged NGINX listens on 8080). Let me know if you’d like me to verify or adjust the Service.

- Result: Rollout succeeded. New pod is Running (app-766ff8b47b-8rpn5); the old pod is terminating.

I fixed it.

- Root cause: The Deployment used an invalid container image tag (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag), causing ImagePullBackOff.
- Change made: Updated the Deployment to use quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest.

results.taskOutput:
I found the cause and fixed it.

What happened:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc".
- Events showed: storageclass.storage.k8s.io "sc" not found and pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.

What I changed:
- Recreated the PVC to use an existing StorageClass "standard" (the cluster’s default local-path provisioner).

Result:
- The PVC is now Bound to a PV.
- The pod homepage-pod in namespace homepage-ns is now Running (1/1) on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane, IP 10.244.0.29.

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), I can switch the PVC to that instead.

outputSteps.content:
I found the cause and fixed it.

What happened:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc".
- Events showed: storageclass.storage.k8s.io "sc" not found and pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.

What I changed:
- Recreated the PVC to use an existing StorageClass "standard" (the cluster’s default local-path provisioner).

Result:
- The PVC is now Bound to a PV.
- The pod homepage-pod in namespace homepage-ns is now Running (1/1) on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane, IP 10.244.0.29.

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), I can switch the PVC to that instead.

results.taskOutput:
I’ve fixed it.

What was wrong
- The nginx container listens on port 8080, but:
  - The Deployment’s readiness/liveness probes were checking port 80 (and paths /is_ready and /get_status).
  - The Service was targeting port 80.
- As a result, the pod never became Ready and the Service sent traffic to a closed port.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment to use port 8080:
  - containerPort 8080
  - readinessProbe and livenessProbe now hit http port 8080 at path /
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service port remains 80 for clients).

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Running and Ready (orders/webapp-…).
- Service Endpoints: healthy, pointing to pod IP on port 8080.
- You can reach it inside the cluster at http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ (or via the Service name http://webapp/ from the same namespace).

How to test quickly
- Port-forward from your machine:
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - Then browse http://localhost:8080
- Or from another pod in the cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run -it --rm tmp --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -sI http://webapp/

Do you need external access (Ingress/LoadBalancer)? I didn’t find an Ingress in orders. I can create an Ingress (with optional TLS) pointing to svc/webapp:80 if you share the hostname you want to use.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I’ve fixed it.

What was wrong
- The nginx container listens on port 8080, but:
  - The Deployment’s readiness/liveness probes were checking port 80 (and paths /is_ready and /get_status).
  - The Service was targeting port 80.
- As a result, the pod never became Ready and the Service sent traffic to a closed port.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment to use port 8080:
  - containerPort 8080
  - readinessProbe and livenessProbe now hit http port 8080 at path /
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service port remains 80 for clients).

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Running and Ready (orders/webapp-…).
- Service Endpoints: healthy, pointing to pod IP on port 8080.
- You can reach it inside the cluster at http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ (or via the Service name http://webapp/ from the same namespace).

How to test quickly
- Port-forward from your machine:
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - Then browse http://localhost:8080
- Or from another pod in the cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run -it --rm tmp --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -sI http://webapp/

Do you need external access (Ingress/LoadBalancer)? I didn’t find an Ingress in orders. I can create an Ingress (with optional TLS) pointing to svc/webapp:80 if you share the hostname you want to use.

- Updated the Deployment to use port 8080:
  - containerPort 8080
  - readinessProbe and livenessProbe now hit http port 8080 at path /
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service port remains 80 for clients).

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Running and Ready (orders/webapp-…).
- Service Endpoints: healthy, pointing to pod IP on port 8080.
- You can reach it inside the cluster at http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ (or via the Service name http://webapp/ from the same namespace).

How to test quickly
- Port-forward from your machine:
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - Then browse http://localhost:8080
- Or from another pod in the cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run -it --rm tmp --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -sI http://webapp/

Do you need external access (Ingress/LoadBalancer)? I didn’t find an Ingress in orders. I can create an Ingress (with optional TLS) pointing to svc/webapp:80 if you share the hostname you want to use.

- Updated the Service in namespace web to:

  - Forward traffic from port 80 to targetPort 8080.

- From any Pod in the cluster:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local
  - or curl http://10.96.68.4

If you need external access
- The Service is ClusterIP (in-cluster only). I can expose it externally by:
  - Creating a NodePort Service, or

namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods.
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Deployment/Pod labels: app=nginx
  - Result: Service had no Endpoints, so traffic couldn’t reach any Pod.
- Additionally, the nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080, while the Service originally targeted port 80.

What I fixed
- Updated the Service in namespace web to:
  - Select the correct Pods (app=nginx).
  - Forward traffic from port 80 to targetPort 8080.

Current state
- Service web/nginx: ClusterIP 10.96.68.4, port 80 -> targetPort 8080, selector app=nginx.
- Endpoints are now populated:

- Deployment is healthy: 1/1 Pod Running.

How to verify in-cluster
- From any Pod in the cluster:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local
  - or curl http://10.96.68.4

If you need external access
- The Service is ClusterIP (in-cluster only). I can expose it externally by:
  - Creating a NodePort Service, or
  - Creating an Ingress (preferred) if an ingress controller is available.

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods.
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Deployment/Pod labels: app=nginx
  - Result: Service had no Endpoints, so traffic couldn’t reach any Pod.
- Additionally, the nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080, while the Service originally targeted port 80.

What I fixed
- Updated the Service in namespace web to:
  - Select the correct Pods (app=nginx).
  - Forward traffic from port 80 to targetPort 8080.

Current state
- Service web/nginx: ClusterIP 10.96.68.4, port 80 -> targetPort 8080, selector app=nginx.
- Endpoints are now populated:
  - 10.244.0.35:8080 (nginx-987f59664-rd4xs)
- Deployment is healthy: 1/1 Pod Running.

How to verify in-cluster
- From any Pod in the cluster:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local
  - or curl http://10.96.68.4

If you need external access
- The Service is ClusterIP (in-cluster only). I can expose it externally by:
  - Creating a NodePort Service, or
  - Creating an Ingress (preferred) if an ingress controller is available.
Tell me which you prefer (and hostname if using Ingress), and I’ll set it up.

results.taskOutput:
Summary of what happened and what I fixed

Root causes
- Pods unschedulable: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node has that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector. Result: no pods, and the Service had no endpoints.
- Port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 by default, while the Service targeted port 80. Even once pods ran, that would have caused connection refused.

Fix applied
- Removed the blocking nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment so it can schedule onto the available node.
- Set the container port to 8080 and added basic readiness/liveness probes.
- Updated the Service to targetPort: 8080 (port remains 80 for clients).
- Verified in-cluster connectivity (curl) returns the nginx HTML.

Current state
- Pods: 2/2 Running and Ready in webshop-frontend.
- Service Endpoints: two backends present on 8080 (e.g., 10.244.0.37:8080, 10.244.0.38:8080).
- In-cluster access to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 returns HTML.

What you’ll see now
- The frontend should stop seeing “connection refused” when calling web-app-service.

If you intended to pin pods to special nodes
- Option A (recommended for now): keep the Deployment without nodeSelector (as it is now).
- Option B: label a node and reintroduce the selector:
  - kubectl label node <your-node> environment=production-gpu
  - Then add spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: { environment: production-gpu } back to the Deployment.

Quick verify commands
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get svc,endpoints web-app-service
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend exec -it <one-web-app-pod> -- curl -sS web-app-service:80 | head

Notes
- I kept the Service client-facing port as 80, mapped to targetPort 8080 in the pod.
- Probes were added so endpoints only register when nginx is actually serving.
- Consider pinning the image to a specific tag (e.g., 1.29 or 1.31) instead of latest for predictable rollouts.

If you want, I can re-add a nodeSelector or Pod affinity as needed once you confirm which nodes should host this workload.

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary of what happened and what I fixed

Root causes
- Pods unschedulable: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node has that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector. Result: no pods, and the Service had no endpoints.
- Port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 by default, while the Service targeted port 80. Even once pods ran, that would have caused connection refused.

Fix applied
- Removed the blocking nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment so it can schedule onto the available node.
- Set the container port to 8080 and added basic readiness/liveness probes.
- Updated the Service to targetPort: 8080 (port remains 80 for clients).
- Verified in-cluster connectivity (curl) returns the nginx HTML.

Current state
- Pods: 2/2 Running and Ready in webshop-frontend.
- Service Endpoints: two backends present on 8080 (e.g., 10.244.0.37:8080, 10.244.0.38:8080).
- In-cluster access to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 returns HTML.

What you’ll see now
- The frontend should stop seeing “connection refused” when calling web-app-service.

If you intended to pin pods to special nodes
- Option A (recommended for now): keep the Deployment without nodeSelector (as it is now).
- Option B: label a node and reintroduce the selector:
  - kubectl label node <your-node> environment=production-gpu
  - Then add spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: { environment: production-gpu } back to the Deployment.

Quick verify commands
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get svc,endpoints web-app-service
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend exec -it <one-web-app-pod> -- curl -sS web-app-service:80 | head

Notes
- I kept the Service client-facing port as 80, mapped to targetPort 8080 in the pod.
- Probes were added so endpoints only register when nginx is actually serving.
- Consider pinning the image to a specific tag (e.g., 1.29 or 1.31) instead of latest for predictable rollouts.

If you want, I can re-add a nodeSelector or Pod affinity as needed once you confirm which nodes should host this workload.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app-deployment
  namespace: webshop-frontend
  labels:
    app: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web-app-container
          image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
          imagePullPolicy: Always
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8080
              protocol: TCP
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: http
            initialDelaySeconds: 2
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: http
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
      # Removed incorrect nodeSelector that prevented scheduling
      restartPolicy: Always
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app-deployment
  namespace: webshop-frontend
  labels:
    app: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web-app-container
          image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
          imagePullPolicy: Always
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8080
              protocol: TCP
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: http
            initialDelaySeconds: 2
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: http
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
      # Removed incorrect nodeSelector that prevented scheduling
      restartPolicy: Always
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

outputSteps.content:
Summary of what happened and what I fixed

Root causes
- Pods unschedulable: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node has that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector. Result: no pods, and the Service had no endpoints.
- Port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 by default, while the Service targeted port 80. Even once pods ran, that would have caused connection refused.

Fix applied
- Removed the blocking nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment so it can schedule onto the available node.
- Set the container port to 8080 and added basic readiness/liveness probes.
- Updated the Service to targetPort: 8080 (port remains 80 for clients).
- Verified in-cluster connectivity (curl) returns the nginx HTML.

Current state
- Pods: 2/2 Running and Ready in webshop-frontend.
- Service Endpoints: two backends present on 8080 (e.g., 10.244.0.37:8080, 10.244.0.38:8080).
- In-cluster access to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 returns HTML.

What you’ll see now
- The frontend should stop seeing “connection refused” when calling web-app-service.

If you intended to pin pods to special nodes
- Option A (recommended for now): keep the Deployment without nodeSelector (as it is now).
- Option B: label a node and reintroduce the selector:
  - kubectl label node <your-node> environment=production-gpu
  - Then add spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: { environment: production-gpu } back to the Deployment.

Quick verify commands
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get svc,endpoints web-app-service
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend exec -it <one-web-app-pod> -- curl -sS web-app-service:80 | head

Notes
- I kept the Service client-facing port as 80, mapped to targetPort 8080 in the pod.
- Probes were added so endpoints only register when nginx is actually serving.
- Consider pinning the image to a specific tag (e.g., 1.29 or 1.31) instead of latest for predictable rollouts.

If you want, I can re-add a nodeSelector or Pod affinity as needed once you confirm which nodes should host this workload.

Done. Here’s what I did and the current state:

- Verified the StorageClass csi-hostpath-sc allows expansion.
- Resized the PVC resize-pv/storage-pvc from 1Gi to 3Gi.
- Observed the controller/node resize flow and restarted the storage-pod to complete the filesystem resize on the node.
- Confirmed:
  - PVC capacity: 3Gi (status.capacity.storage=3Gi)
  - PV capacity: 3Gi
  - Pod storage-pod: Running and reattached to the PVC

Notes:
- With the hostpath CSI driver, df inside the container may show the backing host filesystem (e.g., /dev/root) rather than a 3Gi device, since it can be a bind mount on the host’s root FS. Kubernetes now reflects 3Gi capacity for the claim; if you need an in-container filesystem that reports the exact size, use a storage class/driver that provisions a block device with its own filesystem.

- With the hostpath CSI driver, df inside the container may show the backing host filesystem (e.g., /dev/root) rather than a 3Gi device, since it can be a bind mount on the host’s root FS. Kubernetes now reflects 3Gi capacity for the claim; if you need an in-container filesystem that reports the exact size, use a storage class/driver that provisions a block device with its own filesystem.

- Verified the StorageClass csi-hostpath-sc allows expansion.
- Resized the PVC resize-pv/storage-pvc from 1Gi to 3Gi.

  - PVC capacity: 3Gi (status.capacity.storage=3Gi)
  - PV capacity: 3Gi
  - Pod storage-pod: Running and reattached to the PVC

Notes:
- With the hostpath CSI driver, df inside the container may show the backing host filesystem (e.g., /dev/root) rather than a 3Gi device, since it can be a bind mount on the host’s root FS. Kubernetes now reflects 3Gi capacity for the claim; if you need an in-container filesystem that reports the exact size, use a storage class/driver that provisions a block device with its own filesystem.

All set. I created a secure, multi-tenant setup that meets your requirements. Summary of what’s in place:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled for policy targeting: env=dev for dev-* and dev-shared; env=staging/prod accordingly; dev-shared also labeled role=shared

RBAC
- ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Per-developer full access to own namespace: RoleBinding in each dev namespace binding:
  - User (alice/bob/charlie) → ClusterRole admin
  - Their ServiceAccount → ClusterRole admin
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding users (alice, bob, charlie) and their SAs to ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings (only cluster-admins or explicitly granted users can access)

ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - pods=10, services=5, requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
- dev-shared:
  - pods=20, services=10, requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi
- staging/prod:
  - pods=50, services=20, requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi

Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress + Egress) in all non-system namespaces: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow ingress only from same namespace (intra-namespace)
  - Allow egress to:
    - Same namespace
    - dev-shared (via namespaceSelector role=shared)
    - kube-system (system services; plus explicit DNS to TCP/UDP 53)
- dev-shared:
  - Allow ingress from all dev namespaces (env=dev) and self
  - Egress only to self and kube-system DNS/system services
- staging/prod:
  - Isolated: ingress only from same namespace; egress only to same namespace + kube-system DNS/system services
- System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) untouched by default-deny

Principle of least privilege
- Developers have admin within only their own namespaces and view in dev-shared, with no access to staging/prod
- Cross-developer traffic is blocked; dev namespaces may only reach dev-shared and system services
- staging/prod are isolated from dev

Quick validation commands (optional)
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deployment -n dev-alice --as alice        → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as bob                  → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i create deployment -n dev-shared --as bob         → no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as charlie                 → no
- Network:
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, curl a service in dev-bob              → blocked
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, curl a service in dev-shared           → allowed
  - From a test pod in staging, curl a service in dev-shared             → blocked
  - DNS resolution from any namespace                                    → allowed

If you’d like, I can export the manifests as a single YAML bundle for GitOps, or add LimitRanges/PodSecurity settings for stricter defaults.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All set. I created a secure, multi-tenant setup that meets your requirements. Summary of what’s in place:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled for policy targeting: env=dev for dev-* and dev-shared; env=staging/prod accordingly; dev-shared also labeled role=shared

RBAC
- ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Per-developer full access to own namespace: RoleBinding in each dev namespace binding:
  - User (alice/bob/charlie) → ClusterRole admin
  - Their ServiceAccount → ClusterRole admin
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding users (alice, bob, charlie) and their SAs to ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings (only cluster-admins or explicitly granted users can access)

ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - pods=10, services=5, requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
- dev-shared:
  - pods=20, services=10, requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi
- staging/prod:
  - pods=50, services=20, requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi

Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress + Egress) in all non-system namespaces: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow ingress only from same namespace (intra-namespace)
  - Allow egress to:
    - Same namespace
    - dev-shared (via namespaceSelector role=shared)
    - kube-system (system services; plus explicit DNS to TCP/UDP 53)
- dev-shared:
  - Allow ingress from all dev namespaces (env=dev) and self
  - Egress only to self and kube-system DNS/system services
- staging/prod:
  - Isolated: ingress only from same namespace; egress only to same namespace + kube-system DNS/system services
- System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) untouched by default-deny

Principle of least privilege
- Developers have admin within only their own namespaces and view in dev-shared, with no access to staging/prod
- Cross-developer traffic is blocked; dev namespaces may only reach dev-shared and system services
- staging/prod are isolated from dev

Quick validation commands (optional)
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deployment -n dev-alice --as alice        → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as bob                  → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i create deployment -n dev-shared --as bob         → no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as charlie                 → no
- Network:
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, curl a service in dev-bob              → blocked
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, curl a service in dev-shared           → allowed
  - From a test pod in staging, curl a service in dev-shared             → blocked
  - DNS resolution from any namespace                                    → allowed

If you’d like, I can export the manifests as a single YAML bundle for GitOps, or add LimitRanges/PodSecurity settings for stricter defaults.

outputSteps.content:
All set. I created a secure, multi-tenant setup that meets your requirements. Summary of what’s in place:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled for policy targeting: env=dev for dev-* and dev-shared; env=staging/prod accordingly; dev-shared also labeled role=shared

RBAC
- ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Per-developer full access to own namespace: RoleBinding in each dev namespace binding:
  - User (alice/bob/charlie) → ClusterRole admin
  - Their ServiceAccount → ClusterRole admin
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding users (alice, bob, charlie) and their SAs to ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings (only cluster-admins or explicitly granted users can access)

ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - pods=10, services=5, requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
- dev-shared:
  - pods=20, services=10, requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi
- staging/prod:
  - pods=50, services=20, requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi

Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress + Egress) in all non-system namespaces: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow ingress only from same namespace (intra-namespace)
  - Allow egress to:
    - Same namespace
    - dev-shared (via namespaceSelector role=shared)
    - kube-system (system services; plus explicit DNS to TCP/UDP 53)
- dev-shared:
  - Allow ingress from all dev namespaces (env=dev) and self
  - Egress only to self and kube-system DNS/system services
- staging/prod:
  - Isolated: ingress only from same namespace; egress only to same namespace + kube-system DNS/system services
- System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) untouched by default-deny

Principle of least privilege
- Developers have admin within only their own namespaces and view in dev-shared, with no access to staging/prod
- Cross-developer traffic is blocked; dev namespaces may only reach dev-shared and system services
- staging/prod are isolated from dev

Quick validation commands (optional)
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deployment -n dev-alice --as alice        → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as bob                  → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i create deployment -n dev-shared --as bob         → no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as charlie                 → no
- Network:
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, curl a service in dev-bob              → blocked
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, curl a service in dev-shared           → allowed
  - From a test pod in staging, curl a service in dev-shared             → blocked
  - DNS resolution from any namespace                                    → allowed

If you’d like, I can export the manifests as a single YAML bundle for GitOps, or add LimitRanges/PodSecurity settings for stricter defaults.

What I created
- Namespace: statefulset-test
- Headless Service: statefulset-test/db (serviceName used by the StatefulSet)
- StatefulSet: statefulset-test/db with:
  - replicas: 3 (initially)
  - volumeClaimTemplates: 1Gi RWO PVC per pod, mounted at /data
  - container: busybox that ensures /data/test exists with “initial_data” on first start
  - PVC retention policy set to Retain on scale/delete, so data persists

Then I scaled the StatefulSet back down to 1 replica.

Notes
- If your cluster doesn’t have a default StorageClass, the PVCs will stay Pending. In that case, specify storageClassName in the volumeClaimTemplates or set a default StorageClass.
- Each pod writes “initial_data” to /data/test on its first start (and leaves it untouched on subsequent starts).

How to verify quickly
- Check the StatefulSet and pods:
  kubectl -n statefulset-test get sts db
  kubectl -n statefulset-test get pods -l app=db
- Verify the file content on the remaining pod:
  kubectl -n statefulset-test exec -it db-0 -- cat /data/test
  # expected output: initial_data
